title: London's Indian Fine Dining Boom Is Rewriting the City's Food Map
excerpt: As traditional curry houses decline, a wave of ambitious Indian restaurants — led by Michelin-starred chefs and all-women kitchens — is reshaping how London eats.
body:
Walk into Oudh 1722 on Union Street in Borough and the first thing you notice isn't the food — it's the queue. Since chef Aktar Islam opened his London debut in May, tables have been among the hardest reservations in town, with evening bookings vanishing within minutes and diners advised to check back on the day for last-minute releases.

Islam, whose Birmingham flagship Opheem holds two Michelin stars — one of only two Indian restaurants in the UK to achieve the distinction, alongside Mayfair's Gymkhana — has built Oudh 1722 around the refined cooking of the Awadh region of northern India. The restaurant occupies a three-floor listed building in Borough, with an open kitchen and a lounge bar under a hand-painted ceiling on the top floor.

"Not a mouthful missed its mark. Aktar Islam is in London at last and we are blessed to have him."

— Giles Coren, The Times

What the Critics Are Ordering

The menu centres on dum cooking — the slow, dough-sealed technique synonymous with Lucknow, which UNESCO recognised as a Creative City of Gastronomy in 2025. The Infatuation called the oxtail biryani, "laced with sweet carrot and meat so tender it's stopped bothering to hold its shape," an immediate top-five biryani in London. Wallpaper singled out the smoked Wiltshire lamb shoulder baked in a lamb-fat crust, while Quintessentially pointed diners toward the raan e dum pukht — a showpiece lamb shoulder for two, encased in golden pastry.

Street-style starters such as nargisi kofta with soft golden egg yolk and spiced venison, and kakori kebab of finely minced lamb shoulder with chilli and rose, draw from the courtly traditions of the Nawabi period. Giles Coren, reviewing for The Times, gave the cooking an 8.5 out of 10 and the overall score 8.166, describing a lamb brains masala slapped over hot, blistered paratha as "a dish worth making the detour for."

The Decline of the Curry House, the Rise of Something New

Oudh 1722 arrives at a pivotal moment for Indian food in Britain. The number of traditional curry houses has fallen from a peak of roughly 12,000 in 2011 to about 8,000, driven by shifting eating habits, food delivery apps, and Tier 2 visa restrictions that created a shortage of South Asian chefs willing to work for the wages the old model demanded.

But as the flock-wallpapered high street dining rooms thin out, a new generation of ambitious Indian restaurants is flourishing. Asma Khan's Darjeeling Express, which earned an OpenTable Icon award in 2026, has moved into a larger space on Rupert Street in Soho. Khan's all-women kitchen serves recipes from India's royal courts — dishes passed down orally and extremely rare on restaurant menus anywhere in the world.

The Tamil Prince and its growing chain of spinoffs — Tamil Crown and the newly opened Tamila in Soho — are bringing the food of Tamil Nadu to neighbourhoods across the capital. Co-founder Prince Durairaj opened the Soho flagship on Poland Street in February, with dishes like Thanjavur chicken curry, Chettinad lamb curry, and made-to-order rotis.

Beyond Indian: London's Broader Food Moment

Indian cuisine is part of a broader wave reshaping London's restaurant scene in 2026. Hoppers, the Sri Lankan and South Indian restaurant from the team behind Gymkhana, has launched its fourth outpost in Shoreditch, adding new South Indian influences to its menu of lacy fermented rice pancakes. Kricket continues to draw queues for its samphire pakoras and Keralan fried chicken. And Borough Market, London's oldest food market with roots stretching back to the 12th century, remains a mandatory first stop for any visiting foodie.

The broader restaurant scene is equally energetic. July alone has seen openings from Langosteria at Raffles London, Greek-Cypriot taverna Zylia in Covent Garden, and Turkish-Cypriot newcomer Kismet in Borough. But it is the depth and diversity of South Asian dining — from £5 naan wraps at Baban's to the £100-a-head feasting menus at Oudh 1722 — that sets London apart from every other Western capital.

A Diaspora Diner's Guide

For Indian visitors and the diaspora, London's food scene now presents a paradox: the best Indian food outside South Asia, served in a city where the old curry house is fading. The new restaurants demand a different approach — reservations booked weeks in advance, tasting menus that run north of £70 per person, and dishes that may bear little resemblance to what your neighbourhood curry house served.

At Gymkhana in Mayfair, two Michelin stars guarantee a formal experience. At Darjeeling Express, the warmth of home cooking meets royal court recipes. At Dishoom, the Irani café nostalgia of Bombay lives on across six London locations. And at Oudh 1722, the slow-cooked traditions of Lucknow get their most high-profile London stage yet.

"Soho has always felt like a playground for some of London's most exciting and much-loved restaurants, so opening here has been a real dream of mine."

— Prince Durairaj, Co-founder of Tamila

What's Next

The pipeline shows no signs of slowing. BKC — Biryani Kebab Chai — is bringing Awadhi cuisine to Marble Arch. Chet Sharma, the chef behind Michelin-starred BiBi, is creating the snacks menu for new Mayfair martini bar Brutes of Mayfair. And Hoppers founder Karan Gokani has said he has "never been more excited about a restaurant opening" than the Shoreditch expansion.

For a city where the old narrative was one of decline — fewer curry houses, a brain drain of South Asian chefs — the reality in 2026 tells a different story. London's Indian food scene is not shrinking. It is transforming, trading volume for ambition and nostalgia for innovation. The next time you book a flight to Heathrow, bring an appetite.
